hook: No scientist has ever seen one alive in the wild.

story.text: In 1992, researchers in a remote Vietnamese village found a skull with two long, parallel horns — a large mammal completely new to science.
The saola wears a rich brown coat with white markings across its face, and both sexes carry horns up to twenty inches long.
They call it the Asian unicorn — not because it has one horn, but because almost no one has ever seen it.
No biologist has ever confirmed seeing one alive in the wild, and there is not a single saola in any zoo on Earth.
The most recent photograph of a wild saola was taken by an automatic camera in 2013, standing in a forest creek.
The threat is not even aimed at it: wire snares made from bicycle brake cable, laid by the hundreds for other animals, empty the forest of everything that walks.
The search continues with camera traps, environmental DNA — even the blood meals of forest leeches.
There is room for hope: as little as two percent of its possible range has ever been properly searched.
Vietnam and Laos are building the first conservation breeding center for Annamite wildlife, with the saola as its flagship.
To witness the saola is to keep a place in the world for an animal that may yet walk out of the forest.

editorial.notes: Card v2 drafted from verified Saola Foundation and Re:wild pages. Population honestly uncertain: no confirmed detection since 2013; live sources range from a few individuals to fewer than 50 — card uses the Saola Foundation's phrasing. Lifespan unknown (no saola has ever been kept in captivity). Region circles are broad Annamite generalizations; no locality data exists or is published.

stats.lifespan: Unknown — none ever kept in captivity

reproduction.text: Almost nothing is known. Single calves are the norm, and saola live alone except for mothers with young — nearly every other fact about how the species breeds is still waiting to be learned.

insight.text: Since its discovery in 1992, the saola has been photographed in the wild only five times.
